The hero relies on a dark dusk image with a heavy dark treatment. The villa is attractive, but much of its architecture, landscaping and setting are difficult to inspect, especially in the lower half of the frame.
dailyQueue.evidence: Desktop and mobile screenshots both show substantial areas of near-black foliage and a low-light property image. The mobile crop loses most of the wider site context.
dailyQueue.expected: Premium real estate imagery should feel aspirational while still allowing prospective buyers to assess the actual home, surroundings and quality of light.
dailyQueue.observed: The hero reads more like a cinematic brand backdrop than a high-value property discovery signal.
dailyQueue.recommendation: Use a brighter, higher-resolution hero image with clearer architectural detail and a lighter, more controlled overlay. Preserve the evening mood only if the property remains fully legible.
dailyQueue.title: Hero imagery is dramatic but not sufficiently inspectable

dailyQueue.detail: The opening screen gives visitors no immediate property-search affordance beyond a generic Explore Homes link. There is no visible price, location, bedroom, property-type or availability filter to begin the discovery-to-enquiry journey.
dailyQueue.evidence: The screenshots show only the Explore Homes CTA in the hero. The DOM reports one form overall, but no search controls are visible in the first viewport and the primary goal is a property enquiry.
dailyQueue.expected: A premium property platform should offer a low-friction route from aspiration to a relevant shortlist, with search or clear entry points for browsing by area and requirement.
dailyQueue.location: Homepage hero and opening content section
dailyQueue.observed: The user must commit to a generic browse action before expressing intent or seeing how the inventory is curated.
dailyQueue.recommendation: Add a compact search or discovery bar immediately after or over the hero with area, property type, budget and bedrooms, plus a visible private-search enquiry route for buyers with more specific needs.
dailyQueue.title: Property discovery starts too generically

dailyQueue.recommendation: Define the page’s single primary conversion action and make it explicit in the hero/navigation with business-specific wording.
dailyQueue.expected: At least one obvious primary commercial action

dailyQueue.detail: The primary enquiry path is present but visually secondary to the brand treatment and browsing CTA. The hero does not clearly articulate why a buyer should contact Marbella For Sale now or what response they will receive.
dailyQueue.evidence: The scan identifies contact signals such as Speak to an advisor and Begin a private search, but the screenshots foreground the logo and Explore Homes. The hero copy shown on mobile is low contrast and does not provide a concrete enquiry promise.
dailyQueue.expected: The critical journey should make expert contact feel immediate, credible and specific, with a clear expectation such as tailored recommendations, off-market access or a response timeframe.
dailyQueue.observed: Enquiry is available in navigation and downstream content, but the value exchange is not explicit at the point of highest attention.
dailyQueue.recommendation: Give the enquiry CTA equal first-viewport prominence to discovery and pair it with concise, concrete supporting copy explaining the advisory service and next step.
dailyQueue.title: Enquiry value proposition is under-communicated

issues.detail: The primary availability form does not establish a clear reservation path. It collects dates and a vehicle, but the dominant action is “CHECK AVAILABILITY,” and the scan reports bookingSignalCount 0. There is no visible price calculation, confirmation state or clearly described enquiry handoff in the first interaction.
issues.evidence: The screenshots show From, To and Vehicle fields followed by “CHECK AVAILABILITY.” The automated scan reports bookingSignalCount 0, while the business primary goal is reservation/enquiry. The supporting text says dates and final terms are confirmed directly by Mfinity.
issues.expected: Make the next step explicit: either return live availability and a quote, or clearly route the completed request into a reservation enquiry with the customer’s contact details and a stated response expectation.
issues.observed: The user is asked to check availability but is not told what happens after submission or how the request becomes a booking.
issues.recommendation: Rename and structure the flow around the actual operational model, for example “Request availability” with name, phone/WhatsApp and email fields, selected vehicle, dates and a success confirmation. If instant booking is intended, show rates, deposit and confirmation steps.
issues.title: The booking journey stops before a meaningful reservation action

issues.detail: The hero uses a heavily blurred, low-detail image of a Ferrari. The vehicle is only partially visible and the background dominates the first impression, which weakens the cinematic luxury positioning and makes the actual product difficult to inspect.
issues.evidence: Desktop and mobile screenshots show the car cropped to the lower/right portion of the frame, with the entire background rendered soft and indistinct. The niche explicitly requires vehicle photography, while the first viewport should communicate the vehicle as a premium object.
issues.expected: Use sharp, art-directed vehicle photography with a deliberate crop that clearly shows the car, its finish and silhouette. Preserve atmosphere through lighting and composition rather than applying a level of blur that hides the product.
issues.observed: The background reads more like an abstract colored backdrop than premium car photography.
issues.recommendation: Replace the hero asset with a high-resolution image of a complete hero vehicle in a Marbella-relevant setting. Keep only enough depth-of-field to separate the text from the car, and test the crop independently at desktop and mobile widths.
issues.title: Hero imagery hides the product

issues.detail: Availability and pricing clarity are weak for a luxury rental business. The featured Ferrari panel shows “From €1,400 / day,” but the form does not show a quote, deposit, insurance, mileage, delivery fee or rental conditions, and the copy explicitly defers final terms to direct contact.
issues.evidence: The desktop hero shows one starting daily rate and “Deposit €7,000 · longer rentals on request.” The availability note states that final terms are confirmed directly by Mfinity. No broader pricing or policy summary is visible in the supplied first-view screenshots, and the scan reports no trust signals.
issues.expected: Set expectations before a customer commits contact information. Show the pricing basis, deposit, inclusions and key exclusions near the enquiry action, with transparent qualification where prices vary.
issues.location: Homepage hero and featured vehicle panel
issues.observed: The customer can see an attention-grabbing price but cannot understand the likely total cost or rental requirements.
issues.recommendation: Add a concise pricing and terms layer for each vehicle or enquiry result: daily rate basis, deposit, mileage, insurance, delivery/pickup and minimum rental duration. Use “from” pricing only when the qualification rules are immediately available.
issues.title: Pricing is aspirational but not sufficiently actionable

issues.detail: Trust is underdeveloped for a high-value transaction. The automated scan reports trustSignalCount 0, and the visible reassurance is limited to “regular inspections & maintenance” and direct local contact. There are no customer reviews, fleet standards, insurance explanation, delivery promise, company credentials or clear rental policies in the visible conversion area.
issues.evidence: The mobile screenshot contains the line “Nueva Andalucía base · regular inspections & maintenance · direct local contact,” but no independent proof or specific service commitment. The scan confirms zero detected trust signals.
issues.expected: A luxury rental customer should see credible evidence that the vehicle, payment and handover experience are reliable before submitting a request.
issues.location: Homepage hero and supporting homepage sections
issues.observed: The business asks for a high deposit while providing little visible proof to reduce perceived risk.
issues.recommendation: Add specific trust content near the booking path: verified reviews, fleet condition standards, insurance/deposit explanation, delivery and handover coverage, legal business identity and a direct WhatsApp response promise. Keep claims concrete and verifiable.
issues.title: High-value rental lacks visible trust proof

issues.detail: The page has multiple calls to action with competing labels and no obvious priority between exploration and reservation. “EXPLORE COLLECTION,” “CHECK AVAILABILITY,” “RESERVE NOW,” “RENT ONLINE” and the mobile “WHATSAPP”/“RENT A CAR” controls all appear in or around the hero.
issues.evidence: The desktop screenshot contains at least four prominent action treatments across the navigation, hero form and featured car panel. The scan reports primaryCtaCount 4 and an inconsistentButtonRatio of 0.3333.
issues.expected: A high-converting rental homepage should make the reservation action visually primary and keep discovery as a secondary route. CTA labels should describe distinct outcomes consistently.
issues.location: Header, hero form and featured vehicle module
issues.observed: The user must infer whether “rent online,” “reserve now” and “check availability” are the same or different workflows.
issues.recommendation: Choose one primary conversion label and destination, such as “Request availability.” Make collection browsing secondary, and reserve the featured vehicle CTA for the same selected-vehicle flow rather than presenting it as a separate-looking action.
issues.title: Competing CTAs dilute the conversion path

issues.detail: The mobile hero is vertically overloaded and places the booking form, explanatory copy, operational notes and two large action tiles before the next content section. The result is a long, dense first interaction with little vehicle discovery visible without scrolling.
issues.evidence: In the mobile screenshot, the headline, description, collection CTA, four-field booking form, availability disclaimer, operational note and WhatsApp/Rent a Car tiles occupy nearly the entire captured viewport. The next “VEHICLE CARE” content is visibly clipped at the bottom.
issues.expected: Mobile users should reach a clear vehicle discovery or reservation decision quickly, with the booking action compact and the most important reassurance adjacent to it.
issues.observed: The first screen feels like a stacked form and disclaimer block rather than a focused luxury rental entry point.
issues.recommendation: Prioritize the hero vehicle and one conversion module on mobile. Collapse secondary notes into a concise terms link or disclosure, reduce duplicate action blocks, and expose the first vehicle card or collection cue sooner.
issues.title: Mobile first-view hierarchy is too dense

issues.detail: The hero composition is visually busy because large typography, multiple translucent panels, borders, navigation controls and the darkened car image compete for attention. The desktop form crosses directly over the image while the featured vehicle panel occupies the opposite side.
issues.evidence: The desktop screenshot shows several outlined and translucent rectangles layered over the same photographic area, with the headline, date form, featured vehicle pricing and bottom status bar all active simultaneously.
issues.expected: Luxury interfaces benefit from fewer, more intentional elements with strong spacing and one clear focal point. Overlay panels should support the image rather than fragment it.
issues.observed: The interface feels closer to a stylized template or campaign mockup than a precise rental operation.
issues.recommendation: Reduce simultaneous hero modules, simplify border treatments, and give the vehicle image a clean visual zone. Keep one booking panel and one supporting vehicle detail area with stronger alignment and fewer decorative separators.
issues.title: Hero layering weakens hierarchy

issues.detail: The typography and controls are not fully coherent as a luxury system. The uppercase micro-labels, wide tracking, thin rules, translucent fields and large white rectangular buttons create a repeated visual language, but the components vary in treatment and the scan measures a 33.3% inconsistent button ratio.
issues.evidence: The screenshots show outlined “CONTROL,” outlined “RENT ONLINE,” white filled “CHECK AVAILABILITY,” translucent “RESERVE NOW” and mobile split action tiles with materially different treatments. The scan reports fontFamilyCount 5 and inconsistentButtonRatio 0.3333.
issues.expected: Define a small, deliberate type and control system: one display face, one reading face, a consistent button hierarchy and predictable field styling.
issues.location: Global navigation, hero form and CTA modules
issues.observed: The page has a strong art direction but the component system feels assembled rather than fully resolved.
issues.recommendation: Reduce the number of font roles, normalize button height, border, casing and emphasis, and reserve the filled treatment for the single primary reservation action. Validate contrast and rhythm at both breakpoints.
issues.title: Component styling feels less resolved than the art direction

issues.detail: The copy establishes mood but provides limited decision-making information. “Luxury in every kilometer” and “Keep the feeling” are polished slogans, yet they do not differentiate Mfinity's service, explain delivery coverage, clarify the fleet, or communicate why a customer should choose it over other Marbella rental providers.
issues.evidence: The visible copy is primarily headline, location descriptor and broad category language: “Supercars, performance cars and premium mobility for Marbella and the Costa del Sol.” The content score is 91.67, but that is not evidence that the positioning is reference quality; the screenshots show limited concrete service detail.
issues.expected: Keep the editorial tone while pairing it with specific, locally relevant reasons to book: airport or hotel delivery, Puerto Banús coverage, response time, fleet condition, concierge support and transparent rental standards.
issues.location: Homepage hero and introductory collection section
issues.observed: The page communicates atmosphere more effectively than a differentiated service proposition.
issues.recommendation: Rewrite supporting copy around concrete customer outcomes and service proof. Reserve the slogan for brand expression and use adjacent copy to answer where, how quickly and under what terms Mfinity delivers the rental.
issues.title: Brand language outweighs useful service information

issues.detail: The contact presentation is less premium than the positioning. A Gmail address is shown as the business email, and the page uses “Availability enquiry” rather than giving a clear service response commitment.
issues.evidence: The scan identifies `Mfinity.info@gmail.com` as the email contact. The mobile screenshot uses the wording “Availability enquiry. Dates and final terms are confirmed directly by Mfinity.”
issues.expected: A luxury local operator should present a branded domain email and a concrete, confidence-building response expectation.
issues.observed: The contact details introduce an informal signal beside a €7,000 deposit and premium positioning.
issues.recommendation: Use a branded email address on the Mfinity domain, state the expected reply time and clarify whether WhatsApp, phone or web enquiry is the preferred booking channel.
issues.title: Contact details reduce perceived premium credibility

aiReview.summary: Mfinity has a strong cinematic direction and a technically clean, responsive foundation, but the visual polish currently overstates the operational maturity of the rental experience. The blurred hero hides the product, the booking action does not clearly progress into a reservation or enquiry, pricing and terms remain incomplete, and visible trust proof is absent. The result feels like a stylish launch concept rather than a reference-quality Marbella luxury rental service. The highest-value work is to sharpen the vehicle photography, make the booking handoff explicit, clarify total rental expectations and add credible trust signals without increasing hero density.
strengths: The business and location are immediately legible: Mfinity, Marbella, Nueva Andalucía and Costa del Sol are all present in the first viewport.
The page uses vehicle-led imagery, exposes a fleet route and includes vehicle-specific detail pages, supporting the secondary vehicle-discovery goal.
The availability form is visible immediately on both desktop and mobile and includes dates plus vehicle selection.
The visual language is confidently dark, cinematic and restrained in color, which is directionally appropriate for luxury automotive rental.

The objective scan indicates strong baseline execution: no horizontal overflow, no broken internal links, no console errors, complete image alt coverage, responsive viewport metadata and fast loading performance.

issues.detail: The primary visit journey is not actionable from the first viewport. The hero offers “VISÍTANOS HOY” as a text link, but no address, opening hours, phone number, map action, reservation/contact shortcut, or other visit-specific information is visible.
issues.evidence: Desktop and mobile screenshots show the “VISÍTANOS HOY” CTA, while the objective scan reports bookingSignalCount: 0 and the visible contact path is primarily a generic “Contacto” link.
issues.expected: A premium local café should make the next physical action immediate: show the Puerto Banús address and hours near the hero or in a persistent visit module, with clear map, call, WhatsApp, or directions actions.
issues.location: Homepage hero, desktop and mobile first viewport
issues.observed: The user must click through to discover basic visit logistics.
issues.recommendation: Add a concise location-and-hours block to the homepage, make “Visit us” resolve directly to directions or a visit section, and expose phone/WhatsApp where appropriate. Keep the generic contact page as a secondary route.
issues.title: The homepage does not convert visit intent into an immediate action

issues.detail: The homepage communicates the sugar-free proposition and general atmosphere, but it does not show enough of the actual pâtisserie selection to support menu or concept discovery. The visible food is distant and partially obscured by the hero copy and dark overlay.
issues.evidence: The screenshots use a wide interior photograph with the pastry case and plated items in the background; the scan reports only 439 words and imageCount: 8, with no visible product selection module in the first viewport.
issues.expected: Product-led café positioning should quickly reveal signature pastries, drinks, or a small curated selection with names, appetizing close-up photography, and a direct path to the full menu.
issues.location: Homepage hero and immediately implied first-screen experience
issues.observed: The site sells the philosophy more strongly than the products visitors will come to buy.
issues.recommendation: Introduce a product-led selection section directly after the hero and use dedicated close-up images of signature items. Make the menu CTA specific enough to communicate what the visitor can discover.
issues.title: The sugar-free concept is clearer than the food offering

issues.detail: The desktop hero has a refined editorial direction, but the photographic treatment is too dark and operational for a premium pâtisserie homepage. The interior dominates while the product case and plated food read as secondary details.
issues.evidence: The desktop screenshot shows a dim, wide interior image with heavy dark treatment; pastries are visible but small, reflective, and visually competing with shelving, equipment, ceiling fixtures, and service counters.
issues.expected: Reference-quality premium café imagery should make the actual pastry and café experience immediately desirable, with controlled lighting, intentional composition, and clear product detail.
issues.observed: The first visual impression is a café interior rather than an appetizing premium pastry destination.
issues.recommendation: Use a brighter, more deliberate hero image that includes a clearly inspectable signature product or a stronger product-and-venue composition. Reserve wide interior imagery for a later venue section.
issues.title: Hero imagery under-delivers on appetite and product luxury

issues.detail: The mobile hero crop prioritizes the ceiling and upper shelving, leaving the strongest food content low in the frame and partially hidden behind the headline. This weakens the first-screen product signal and makes the composition feel like a desktop image forced into a narrow viewport.
issues.evidence: In the mobile screenshot, the upper half is largely ceiling and cabinetry; the pastry case begins around the middle, while the drink and plated food are cropped at the right and bottom edges.
issues.expected: A mobile-specific crop should preserve a recognizable pastry, beverage, or inviting customer-facing venue detail behind the copy, with enough breathing room for the headline and CTA.
issues.observed: The mobile first impression is less appetizing and less intentional than the desktop version.
issues.recommendation: Provide a mobile-specific focal crop or alternate portrait image. Reposition the visual subject so the product remains legible without competing with the headline, CTA, and footer metadata.
issues.title: Mobile image art direction loses the product signal

issues.detail: The contact route is visually prominent, but it is generic and does not communicate the preferred action for a local hospitality business. There is no visible phone, map, reservation, or messaging option in the supplied first viewport.
issues.evidence: The header contains a pill-shaped “CONTACTO” button on desktop and mobile, while the scan finds four contact signals but no booking signal and no form.
issues.expected: The main conversion control should match the business goal and remove ambiguity, such as “Cómo llegar”, “Reservar”, “Llamar”, or “WhatsApp”, supported by contact details and location context.
issues.observed: “Contacto” makes the user choose a generic destination instead of taking the most likely café action.
issues.recommendation: Replace or supplement the generic header CTA with the highest-value local action, and provide direct call/directions/messaging links on mobile. Use “Contacto” for broader enquiries rather than the main visit CTA.
issues.title: The main CTA is generic for a hospitality visit goal

issues.detail: The visual language is premium and distinctive, but the homepage currently reads more like a brand manifesto than a complete Puerto Banús café decision tool. Core local trust signals are not visible at the point of intent.
issues.evidence: The scan reports trustSignalCount: 0. The screenshots show only “MARBELLA · SPAIN” as location context, with no address, hours, reviews, press, awards, social proof, or recognizable founder/product credentials in the first viewport.
issues.expected: A premium destination café should establish why it is worth visiting and make the local context credible through precise location details, operating information, founder or chef authority, and selective proof.
issues.location: Homepage first viewport and primary conversion path
issues.observed: The site establishes aesthetic quality but not enough operational or third-party confidence for a real-world visit decision.
issues.recommendation: Add precise Puerto Banús location information, hours, map/directions, and one or two restrained trust signals such as chef credentials, press, awards, or verified customer/social proof.
issues.title: Premium atmosphere is not yet matched by local trust signals

issues.detail: The first-screen messaging is polished but somewhat abstract and repetitive: “No sugar. Same taste.” and “No se trata de renunciar. Se trata de evolucionar.” reinforce the philosophy without adding concrete reasons to visit, signature products, or proof of quality.
issues.evidence: The H1 and later H2 identified in the scan are both positioning statements; the screenshot hero copy describes a conscious way to enjoy sweets but does not name a product, chef credential, ingredient standard, or customer benefit beyond sugar-free.
issues.expected: Premium positioning should pair the memorable proposition with concrete, credible proof: signature creations, chef authorship, ingredient approach, awards, or a specific reason Puerto Banús visitors should choose this café.
issues.location: Homepage hero and supporting homepage copy
issues.observed: Brand attitude is stronger than tangible differentiation or trust.
issues.recommendation: Keep the concise headline, then add one concrete proof point and one product or experience cue. Use the concept/story pages to deepen the narrative without making the homepage depend on abstract brand language.
issues.title: Positioning lacks concrete proof and product specificity

issues.detail: The navigation is elegant but relies heavily on small uppercase labels and understated links. This creates a premium editorial tone, yet it may reduce scanability and clarity for users seeking practical information quickly, especially on a busy hospitality visit journey.
issues.evidence: The desktop header uses small labels for CONCEPTO, CARTA, ERIC, and VISÍTANOS, while the scan identifies three tiny tap targets and a 12px font size for CARTA, ERIC, and LEGAL.
issues.expected: A high-end interface can remain restrained while giving practical navigation stronger hierarchy, readable sizing, and clear prioritization of menu and visit information.
issues.location: Desktop header navigation and footer utility links
issues.observed: The navigation visually prioritizes atmosphere and brand restraint over rapid task discovery.
issues.recommendation: Increase the usable visual prominence of CARTA and VISÍTANOS, preserve generous hit areas, and make the mobile menu expose menu, location, hours, and contact in a clear order.
issues.title: Editorial navigation treatment weakens practical scanability

aiReview.summary: Zùsto Café has a credible premium identity and a strong initial art direction, supported by excellent measured performance, accessibility, and responsive behavior. The main gap is commercial: the first screen sells the philosophy and atmosphere more effectively than the products or the visit. Product photography, precise local logistics, direct visit actions, and trust signals need to become first-class content. The design is polished, but it is not yet reference quality for a destination pâtisserie because the conversion path remains generic and the mobile hero crop weakens appetite and product clarity.
strengths: The brand proposition is immediately legible: sugar-free pâtisserie with a premium, modern point of view.
The desktop composition has a strong editorial tone, disciplined typography, restrained color treatment, and clear hero hierarchy.
The venue photography gives the business a real physical presence instead of relying on generic decorative imagery.
The homepage provides direct paths to the menu, visit information, and contact, and the technical scan confirms no broken internal links or critical journey failures.
The mobile layout avoids horizontal overflow and preserves the main headline and primary menu CTA at a usable scale.

issues.detail: The hero is visually polished but the proposition remains broad and somewhat abstract for professional buyers evaluating a transport supplier.
issues.evidence: The H1 is “Movilidad turística con presencia.” Supporting copy says “Trenes y tranvías turísticos para ciudades, eventos, ayuntamientos y recintos,” while the hero brief reduces the offer to “Alquiler · venta” and “Proyecto a medida.”
issues.expected: The first viewport should quickly establish what can be commissioned, for whom, and why this supplier is credible in Spain. A buyer should understand the available service model and likely project outcome without interpreting brand language.
issues.location: Homepage hero, especially the H1 and Project Brief block
issues.observed: “Con presencia” is distinctive but not operationally informative. The copy does not immediately distinguish rental, sale, turnkey project delivery, fleet supply, operation, maintenance, or route planning.
issues.recommendation: Keep the distinctive headline as a supporting brand line, but make the primary proposition literal and buyer-oriented. State the core offer, target buyer, geography, and delivery scope in one concise sentence, then expose the principal service paths directly below it.
issues.title: The opening proposition prioritizes atmosphere over service clarity

issues.detail: The homepage has limited visible proof for a high-consideration professional service and does not sufficiently reduce buyer risk.

issues.expected: A reference-quality supplier site should substantiate claims with named case studies, locations, vehicle details, delivery capabilities, and credible proof appropriate to municipalities, event organizers, venues, and tourism operators.
issues.location: Homepage sections following the hero and portfolio discovery journey
issues.observed: The page introduces four audiences, but the screenshot and scan provide little evidence that the company has successfully served them or can execute the stated “proyecto a medida.”
issues.recommendation: Add a structured proof block immediately after the service overview: named Spanish projects, client or municipality names where permitted, routes or passenger capacity, delivery scope, photography of completed work, testimonials, and clear links to detailed case studies. Avoid relying on a single Écija reference as the principal trust signal.
issues.title: Insufficient proof for a specialist supplier

issues.detail: The mobile hero consumes most of the initial journey before the visitor reaches service choice or additional proof, and its large display treatment leaves limited room for decision-making content.
issues.evidence: The mobile screenshot shows the header, hero headline, paragraph, two full-width CTAs, and the entire Project Brief occupying the viewport. The scan records mobile score 80 and a tinyTapTargetRatio of 0.7222 with 19 tiny targets overall.
issues.expected: On mobile, the first screen should establish the offer and provide a decisive enquiry action without requiring users to pass through extensive decorative metadata. Navigation, labels, and supporting content should remain comfortably readable and easy to tap.
issues.location: Mobile homepage hero at approximately 390px viewport width
issues.observed: The hero headline is visually dominant and the two CTAs are usable, but the page delays service discovery and proof. The compact desktop-style labels and navigation conventions also contribute to a dense, small-text experience.
issues.recommendation: Shorten the mobile hero copy, prioritize one primary enquiry CTA, move the project brief below a concise service chooser, and increase or simplify small labels. Ensure the mobile menu exposes direct service and contact routes with generous tap areas.
issues.title: Mobile first-viewport is too long and presentation-heavy

issues.detail: The site presents multiple audiences but does not turn them into clear, mutually exclusive entry points for the critical lead journey.
issues.evidence: The heading structure includes “Ciudades y turismo,” “Eventos y ferias,” “Ayuntamientos,” and “Recintos y empresas,” while the primary navigation separately includes “Trenes turísticos,” “Soluciones,” “Vehículos,” and “Empresa.”
issues.expected: A buyer-facing site should let each audience quickly select a relevant route and see tailored services, proof, and an enquiry prompt. Navigation labels should map cleanly to buyer intent rather than to internal content categories.
issues.location: Homepage audience/service overview and global navigation
issues.observed: There are several plausible paths, but the distinction between Solutions, Vehicles, Trains Turísticos, and the four contexts is not obvious from the first viewport. This creates discovery work before a buyer can form a relevant enquiry.
issues.recommendation: Create a simple audience-led service matrix with one clear destination per buyer type, explain the relationship between vehicle supply and managed projects, and attach a relevant CTA to each path. Keep global navigation to the few routes buyers actually need.
issues.title: Audience segmentation does not resolve into clear buyer paths

issues.detail: The visual system is distinctive in intent but overuses small uppercase labels and editorial framing, creating a presentation layer that competes with practical information.
issues.evidence: The scan reports 5 font families, 35 colors, a tinyTextRatio of 0.3799, 96 tiny-text elements, and 39.1% inconsistent button ratio. The screenshots show 7-11px navigation, kickers, labels, metadata, and footer text alongside a very large serif hero.
issues.expected: Professional-services interfaces should preserve the brand character while maintaining a strict information hierarchy: readable navigation and metadata, fewer type treatments, consistent controls, and clear contrast between display messaging and actionable service information.
issues.location: Global typography, header navigation, hero metadata, and CTA system
issues.observed: The page resembles a premium design portfolio or agency case-study template. “Project Brief / 01,” vertical timeline decoration, dense micro-labels, and mixed serif/sans treatments add style but make the commercial offer harder to scan.
issues.recommendation: Reduce the number of type families and decorative labels, raise navigation and metadata sizes to comfortable reading dimensions, standardize button sizing and casing, and reserve the editorial display treatment for the hero and selected section headings.
issues.title: Editorial styling overwhelms the operational hierarchy

issues.detail: The public-facing site lacks visible legal and privacy reassurance for a Spain-based lead-generation service handling personal enquiry data.
issues.evidence: The scan reports hasPrivacyLink false and hasLegalLink false. The business market is Spain and the stated primary goal is lead generation.
issues.expected: A professional Spanish lead-generation site should expose privacy, legal notice, and consent information at the point of enquiry and in the footer, with clear company identity and contact details.
issues.observed: There is no visible legal/privacy route in the measured page structure, reducing confidence when a prospect is asked to initiate a commercial conversation.
issues.recommendation: Add footer links to Aviso legal, Política de privacidad, and relevant cookie information. Include an explicit consent statement beside any enquiry form and make the operating company identity and registered contact details easy to verify.
issues.title: Legal and privacy trust layer is missing

issues.detail: The page relies on low-size uppercase text for navigation, labels, and actions, which is likely to be difficult to read and weakens inclusive use even where the overall layout is technically stable.
issues.evidence: The scan reports tinyTextRatio 0.3799, 96 tiny-text elements, and examples including 8.5px kickers, 9px CTA text, 9.5px navigation, and 7px brand microcopy. The screenshots visibly show dense, low-scale uppercase labels.
issues.expected: Supporting text and controls should remain readable across desktop and mobile, with sufficient contrast and a clear size hierarchy. Brand microcopy should not carry essential navigation or service meaning.
issues.location: Header, hero kicker, CTA labels, Project Brief, and footer
issues.observed: The visual language is legible at a large desktop screenshot but becomes strained on mobile, where the small labels sit beside large display type and require more effort to parse.
issues.recommendation: Increase functional text sizes, reduce uppercase tracking, use normal-case labels where appropriate, and verify contrast and reading comfort at mobile scale. Remove nonessential microcopy rather than shrinking it further.
issues.title: Functional text is too small for comfortable scanning

topPriority.title: Too many mobile tap targets are undersized

aiReview.summary: Trenes y Tranvías has a memorable, premium visual direction and strong technical foundations, but the experience currently feels closer to a styled brand presentation than a fully convincing specialist-services lead engine. The largest commercial gaps are the lack of an immediate enquiry mechanism, weak visible proof, and an opening proposition that is more poetic than operational. On mobile, oversized editorial typography and a long hero push service selection and evidence too far down the journey. The design should retain its distinctive identity while making scope, credibility, buyer paths, and contact mechanics substantially more explicit.
strengths: The brand has a clear visual point of view: black, warm gold, and a large editorial serif create a recognizable premium transport identity rather than a generic corporate site.
The hero uses an actual tourist train image and immediately names the broad customer contexts: cities, events, municipalities, and venues.
The primary action, “Solicitar presupuesto,” is repeated and visually prominent, with a secondary vehicle-discovery path supporting portfolio exploration.
The layout is structurally disciplined, with one H1, coherent heading progression, no reported broken internal links, and strong measured performance.
The mobile layout preserves the main CTA and converts navigation into a compact menu rather than introducing horizontal overflow.

issues.detail: The first viewport is almost entirely black, with only a barely perceptible background treatment. No yacht, coastline, marina, guest experience, or destination is visible at the decision point.
issues.evidence: Both supplied desktop and mobile screenshots show a dark hero with typography and controls but no inspectable yacht or Marbella/Puerto Banus visual. The scan also reports only 6 images across the page.
issues.expected: A reference-quality luxury charter site opens with a cinematic, clearly readable image or film frame of the actual fleet in its local setting, while retaining disciplined text contrast and legibility.
issues.location: Homepage hero, desktop and mobile first viewport
issues.observed: The page communicates editorial luxury through black space and type, but not the product being sold. It could plausibly belong to a luxury travel, property, or concierge brand.
issues.recommendation: Replace the near-black hero treatment with an art-directed, high-resolution fleet or on-water Marbella image/video still. Keep the dark overlay only as strong as necessary for the copy, and ensure the vessel, water and destination remain visibly legible.
issues.title: The hero hides the product rather than selling the yacht experience

issues.detail: The prominent enquiry module looks like a booking configurator but does not communicate interaction state, inventory context, or what happens after submission.
issues.evidence: The desktop module presents fixed values for guests, date, duration, departure and occasion; the main action says “FIND MY CHARTER.” On mobile, the selector grid ends with a large empty-looking cell next to “Private yacht day,” and the CTA appears as a separate black row. The scan confirms a form and booking signals, but no availability signal beyond a reassurance statement.
issues.expected: Luxury charter conversion should make the next step explicit: select a real date and party details, receive matched yachts or submit an availability request, with a concise service expectation.
issues.observed: The control surface is visually polished but ambiguous. The large blank mobile cell reads as unfinished layout rather than a purposeful control, which undermines confidence at the primary conversion moment.
issues.recommendation: Make each field visibly selectable with value affordances and clear required/optional states. Remove or fill the empty grid cell, and relabel the action to describe the outcome, such as “Check availability” or “Request tailored options,” with a short response-time promise nearby.
issues.title: Primary booking path has an elegant but unclear interaction model

issues.detail: The opening claim is evocative but gives little immediate evidence of the fleet quality, charter range, or commercial substance behind the premium positioning.
issues.evidence: The hero headline is “Marbella, from the water.” Supporting copy groups private yacht charter, sailing, fishing and group experiences together. The only visible pricing context in the desktop screenshot is small footer-like text: “Sunseeker 68 · from €4,375 / 4h,” which disappears from the shown mobile viewport.
issues.expected: An exclusive yacht-charter proposition should rapidly establish the actual calibre of yacht, charter occasions, service inclusions, and a price starting point in a way that supports qualification without feeling transactional.
issues.observed: “Yacht charter,” “sailing,” “fishing,” and “group experiences” broaden the offer, but the presentation does not resolve whether this is a high-end yacht specialist or a general activity operator. Key commercial proof is too secondary.
issues.recommendation: Bring a concise fleet/value qualifier into the hero or immediately below it: flagship vessel class, private crew/skipper positioning, service inclusions, and a visible “from” price or transparent pricing route. Separate yacht-charter positioning from activity-led offers in the information hierarchy.
issues.title: Luxury positioning is not substantiated early enough

issues.detail: The visible trust treatment relies on generic claims rather than proof that reduces the risk of an expensive charter enquiry.
issues.evidence: Visible reassurance messages are “15+ years local experience,” “Real availability checked directly by the team,” and “Qualified skipper included with charters.” The objective scan records zero trust signals.
issues.expected: Reference-quality charter sites show verifiable proof appropriate to a considered travel purchase: guest ratings or selected testimonials, licensing/insurance and professional membership where applicable, named local expertise, or credible partner/press recognition.
issues.location: Homepage reassurance strip below charter finder
issues.observed: The claims are relevant but anonymous and repetitive in tone. They state benefits without giving a prospect a reason to verify or believe them.
issues.recommendation: Retain the operational reassurances, but add attributable, specific proof close to the enquiry path: review source and score, real guest quotation, licensing/insurance credentials, and/or named captain or concierge credentials.
issues.title: Trust claims lack supporting evidence

issues.detail: The mobile header and fixed conversion controls consume substantial vertical space before a user can assess the offer, while the menu control is visually oversized relative to the secondary contact action.
issues.evidence: In the mobile screenshot, the header is approximately 150px high and contains a large circular menu button; the logo, phone number and button compete for the same narrow top band. The enquiry panel and fixed two-button footer occupy much of the remaining viewport.
issues.expected: Premium mobile craft keeps the brand and immediate conversion route available without pushing product imagery, fleet evidence, or essential charter details below the fold.
issues.observed: The composition is clean, but it is vertically expensive. The visible screen becomes dominated by chrome, a text-only hero and the form shell rather than the charter proposition.
issues.recommendation: Reduce the mobile header height and menu control diameter, use a compact sticky enquiry affordance, and reserve first-screen space for a visible yacht image plus the primary charter decision. Keep WhatsApp as a secondary, clearly labelled contact route rather than co-equal persistent emphasis.
issues.title: Mobile first viewport is dominated by interface chrome

issues.detail: The site mixes refined display typography with several small, tightly tracked utility labels and inconsistent CTA treatments, creating moments that feel more like a design-system demonstration than a fully resolved luxury brand.
issues.evidence: The scan finds 3 font families, 38 colors, a 22.7% inconsistent button ratio, and 10 visible tiny-text instances. In the screenshots, labels such as “GUESTS,” “DATE,” and “FIND MY CHARTER” use conspicuously different casing, tracking and tonal rules; desktop uses a pill “Plan a charter,” whereas mobile uses bordered rectangular “Plan a charter” and “WhatsApp” buttons.
issues.expected: A high-end editorial system uses a restrained type scale and a small, deliberately repeated set of action styles. Utility text remains comfortably readable and clearly subordinate, not visually fragmented.
issues.location: Header, charter finder, reassurance strip and mobile fixed actions
issues.observed: The main serif headline is strong, but the supporting system has too many competing text voices and button geometries for the level of polish implied by the positioning.
issues.recommendation: Consolidate utility label styles, raise the smallest visible type where possible, and define one primary CTA and one secondary-contact treatment that remain consistent across breakpoints. Reduce unnecessary color and type variation in the booking module.
issues.title: Supporting design system is less resolved than the hero type

aiReview.summary: This is a polished dark editorial foundation with a clear route to enquiry, but it currently communicates an abstract luxury brand more effectively than a premium Marbella yacht charter. The largest commercial gap is the invisible product: first-view imagery, fleet proof, pricing context and verifiable trust need to carry much more of the experience. Resolve the ambiguous booking interaction and simplify mobile chrome, then the visual language can credibly support the luxury positioning rather than merely signal it.
strengths: The desktop hero has disciplined spacing, strong contrast and a memorable editorial headline treatment.
The charter finder is placed immediately after the proposition, so the primary journey is visible without scrolling.
The local focus is explicit: Marbella, Puerto Banus and Costa del Sol are present in the first message, and departure context is built into the enquiry surface.
The page has a clear desktop navigation model, contact number, direct enquiry route and mobile WhatsApp option.
The supplied mobile layout avoids horizontal overflow and maintains large, touch-friendly primary actions.

aiReview.summary: Marbella For Sale has a strong visual starting point and technically clean delivery, but the experience currently over-invests in cinematic brand atmosphere relative to the commercial job of helping a buyer discover and enquire about a property. The most material gaps are inspectability of the hero imagery, inefficient mobile opening hierarchy, generic discovery entry, limited visible proof of local expertise and an unclear Control Panel utility. It feels polished and intentional, but not yet reference-quality for premium real estate because the luxury promise is asserted more strongly than it is evidenced.
strengths: The visual direction has a credible premium foundation: restrained typography, a cinematic property-led hero and a calm dark-to-light palette.
The homepage establishes the brand and market immediately, with Marbella For Sale prominent in the opening frame and a clear Explore Homes route.
The information architecture supports the core real-estate needs through properties, developments, areas, guides, selling and contact routes.

The responsive implementation is structurally sound in the supplied evidence: no horizontal overflow, no broken internal links, no console errors, zero CLS and strong desktop/mobile loading measurements.
The property imagery is relevant to the niche and the saved-property affordance supports repeat browsing.

issues.title: Cookie dialog blocks the primary conversion experience
issues.detail: The cookie/privacy dialog appears immediately over the hero and covers a substantial portion of the first viewport. On desktop it obscures the lower-right hero and competes directly with the “RESERVAR MESA” action. On mobile it covers the main H1 and the next part of the hero entirely.
issues.evidence: Desktop screenshot: the dialog occupies the lower-right area and overlaps the hero CTA region. Mobile screenshot: the dialog begins around the middle of the viewport, covering “Mar de verdad.” and most of the first-screen content. The objective scan confirms a first-visit modal is present despite the critical journey technically succeeding.
issues.observed: The visitor must resolve a large privacy interaction before they can understand the offer or act on the reservation CTA. The modal has greater visual weight than the product message.
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution should preserve the reservation journey and the restaurant proposition in the first viewport. Consent UI should be compact, strategically positioned, and should never conceal the H1 or primary booking action, especially on mobile.
issues.location: Initial hero viewport, desktop and mobile; cookie/privacy dialog.
issues.recommendation: Reduce the consent surface to a compact bottom sheet or narrow banner, keep the hero H1 and booking action unobstructed, and use a clear primary consent button with secondary settings access. On mobile, reserve space below the hero content or delay nonessential presentation until the user has seen the proposition.

issues.title: The reservation path is prominent in navigation but weak inside the visible hero
issues.detail: The primary business goal is reservation, yet the main hero booking action is visually subordinate to the background and becomes effectively unavailable when the cookie dialog is shown. The desktop header reservation control is stronger than the hero CTA, while the mobile screenshot shows only the top reservation button before the modal interrupts the journey.
issues.evidence: Desktop screenshot: “RESERVAR MESA” has low contrast against the image and sits behind the privacy dialog's visual field. The scan reports 7 primary CTA signals and 5 booking signals, but the screenshot shows no unobstructed, high-confidence booking path through the hero.
issues.observed: Reservation exists, but the visual priority is not consistently maintained across the first viewport.
issues.expected: A premium restaurant homepage should make booking feel immediate and inevitable: one dominant, high-contrast reservation action should remain visible without dismissal or interpretation.
issues.location: Hero lower-left CTA and top navigation reservation button.
issues.recommendation: Give the hero CTA a stronger contrast treatment, keep it clear of overlays, and consider adding a concise booking reassurance such as availability, booking platform, or response expectation near the action. Ensure the mobile sticky/header reservation control remains visible without competing with the consent UI.

issues.title: Mobile first-viewport hierarchy is disrupted by the privacy overlay
issues.detail: The mobile composition places the location label and H1 low in the viewport, then the dialog covers the headline before the user can read the proposition. The result is a partially visible headline with no usable hero CTA in the screenshot.
issues.evidence: Mobile screenshot: the H1 is visible only as “Mar de” before being covered by the dialog. The privacy panel occupies most of the lower half of the screen and extends to the viewport edges with substantial internal spacing.
issues.observed: The page appears visually broken or incomplete at first load, even though the underlying responsive layout has no overflow according to the scan.
issues.expected: The first mobile viewport should show the restaurant identity, proposition and booking action in a stable, readable sequence. Overlays must not create apparent clipping or hide primary content.
issues.location: Mobile hero and cookie dialog at approximately 780px viewport width.
issues.recommendation: Shorten the mobile consent copy and reduce modal height substantially. Position it as a compact bottom consent bar or ensure the full hero proposition remains above it. Verify the resulting layout at common 360px, 390px and 430px widths.

issues.title: The hero sells atmosphere more effectively than the restaurant's actual offer
issues.detail: The hero communicates a beautiful waterfront setting, but it does not quickly establish what La Bocana is known for, what guests will eat, or why it is worth choosing over other premium restaurants in Puerto Banús. “Mar de verdad.” is evocative but abstract.
issues.evidence: The visible hero contains the H1 “Mar de verdad.” and supporting copy about Mediterranean cuisine and recognizable product, but the image is dominated by table setting, chairs and waterfront ambience rather than a dish, chef, signature product or distinctive dining moment.
issues.observed: The first viewport creates mood but leaves the core value proposition under-specified. The positioning “premium waterfront restaurant” is implied rather than made concrete.
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution should pair atmosphere with a specific appetite and differentiation signal: signature seafood, Mediterranean product, a recognizable dish, chef point of view, or a clear reason to reserve now.
issues.location: Hero headline, supporting paragraph and background image.
issues.recommendation: Keep the poetic headline but strengthen the supporting message with a specific culinary promise and visible product evidence. Use an editorial food or service image in the first sequence, or introduce a signature dish/product panel immediately after the hero.

issues.title: The hero image is atmospheric but soft and insufficiently appetizing
issues.detail: The selected image communicates place and table styling, but the crop is visually busy and lacks a clear focal subject. On mobile it becomes noticeably soft and enlarged, with tablecloth, chairs and glassware dominating the frame.
issues.evidence: Desktop screenshot: the image is darkened and several chairs, glasses, foliage and table surfaces compete for attention. Mobile screenshot: the crop magnifies the background and produces a blurred composition; no food is visible in either screenshot.
issues.observed: The visual quality supports lifestyle positioning but does not deliver the appetite, product clarity or photographic distinctiveness expected from a premium restaurant.
issues.expected: Reference-quality restaurant imagery should make the food, ingredients, service or signature setting inspectable. Mobile crops should retain a deliberate focal point rather than simply enlarging the desktop composition.
issues.location: Full-bleed hero background, especially the mobile crop.
issues.recommendation: Replace or supplement the hero with sharper, higher-resolution photography featuring a signature dish, seafood/product detail or a clearly staged waterfront dining moment. Define an intentional mobile focal position and test the crop at the actual mobile viewport.

issues.title: Trust proof is too thin for a premium destination restaurant
issues.detail: The visible experience provides almost no third-party or operational proof that validates the premium positioning. The objective scan reports only one trust signal.
issues.evidence: The scan records trustSignalCount: 1. The mobile screenshot shows “BEST OF THE BEST 2025,” but there are no visible review signals, ratings, press mentions, chef credentials, reservation-partner proof or meaningful guest reassurance in the first viewport.
issues.observed: The brand asks visitors to infer quality from art direction alone. That is insufficient for a destination market where diners compare venues before reserving.
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution should combine visual aspiration with concise proof: award attribution, review rating, press recognition, chef/product credentials, or a credible reservation and cancellation policy signal.
issues.recommendation: Make the award or recognition explicit and attributable, then add one or two restrained trust modules near the booking path. Avoid generic badges; use verifiable source, year and context where available.

issues.title: Menu discovery is available but not prioritized as a decision aid
issues.detail: The menu is present in the navigation, but the first viewport does not provide a visible route to inspect dishes, price level or culinary style beyond the abstract supporting copy.
issues.evidence: The scan lists `/carta` as an internal link, but the screenshot shows only the top navigation link “CARTA”; there is no hero-level menu prompt, featured dish, menu excerpt or pricing cue.
issues.observed: Visitors evaluating whether the restaurant fits their taste, occasion or budget must discover the menu through navigation before they have enough information to commit to a reservation.
issues.expected: Premium restaurant sites should let users move naturally between appetite-building and reservation, with menu discovery close to the primary booking path.
issues.recommendation: Add a secondary “Ver la carta” action or a featured signature dish/product teaser directly beneath or beside the reservation CTA, while keeping reservation as the dominant action.

issues.title: Operational reassurance is not visible early enough
issues.detail: Key practical details such as opening hours and reservation expectations are not visible in the first viewport. These details are important for visitors making a time-sensitive booking decision in a destination market.
issues.evidence: The screenshot shows location and phone contact in the header, but no opening hours, service periods, booking conditions or arrival guidance. The scan identifies contact signals but does not identify visible hours or a first-viewport operational reassurance signal.
issues.observed: The site establishes mood before answering basic planning questions that commonly precede a reservation.
issues.expected: Reference-quality execution should surface location, hours or service windows, and a concise booking reassurance near the reservation route without making the page feel administrative.
issues.location: Hero, header and immediately subsequent content.
issues.recommendation: Add service hours or a compact “Horario / Cómo llegar” utility near the booking action or in the first post-hero section. Keep it scannable and link the location directly to maps.

issues.title: The navigation is polished but dense for the desktop header
issues.detail: The desktop header carries logo, four main navigation items, consultation link, language control, phone number and reservation button over a photographic background. The resulting hierarchy is compressed and some labels read as equally prominent.
issues.evidence: Desktop screenshot: “CONSULTAR RESERVA,” phone number, language control and “RESERVAR” compete across the right side of a single header row. The scan reports 17 navigation links and a 42.86% inconsistent-button ratio, indicating several CTA treatments are not fully standardized.
issues.observed: The header feels closer to a brand showcase than an effortlessly scannable booking utility. The reservation action is present but surrounded by multiple competing controls.
issues.expected: Reference-quality navigation should establish a clear order: brand, menu/experience discovery, contact/location utility, then one unmistakable reservation action.
issues.recommendation: Reduce competing text density, visually demote consultation and phone utilities, and standardize CTA styling so the reservation control is the singular dominant action. Preserve the mobile header's strong reservation affordance.

topPriority.title: Cookie dialog blocks the primary conversion experience
topPriority.detail: The cookie/privacy dialog appears immediately over the hero and covers a substantial portion of the first viewport. On desktop it obscures the lower-right hero and competes directly with the “RESERVAR MESA” action. On mobile it covers the main H1 and the next part of the hero entirely.
topPriority.evidence: Desktop screenshot: the dialog occupies the lower-right area and overlaps the hero CTA region. Mobile screenshot: the dialog begins around the middle of the viewport, covering “Mar de verdad.” and most of the first-screen content. The objective scan confirms a first-visit modal is present despite the critical journey technically succeeding.
topPriority.observed: The visitor must resolve a large privacy interaction before they can understand the offer or act on the reservation CTA. The modal has greater visual weight than the product message.
topPriority.expected: Reference-quality execution should preserve the reservation journey and the restaurant proposition in the first viewport. Consent UI should be compact, strategically positioned, and should never conceal the H1 or primary booking action, especially on mobile.
topPriority.location: Initial hero viewport, desktop and mobile; cookie/privacy dialog.
topPriority.recommendation: Reduce the consent surface to a compact bottom sheet or narrow banner, keep the hero H1 and booking action unobstructed, and use a clear primary consent button with secondary settings access. On mobile, reserve space below the hero content or delay nonessential presentation until the user has seen the proposition.

aiReview.summary: La Bocana has a strong premium visual direction: restrained typography, waterfront imagery, clear location cue and a prominent reservation action. However, the first-visit experience is materially weakened by the oversized cookie dialog, which obscures the hero message and reservation CTA on desktop and covers the main headline on mobile. The imagery is atmospheric but does not sufficiently communicate food, product quality or the restaurant's distinctive offer. The site currently feels like a polished brand concept more than a fully convincing premium-restaurant conversion experience.
strengths: The waterfront setting is immediately legible and relevant to Puerto Banús / Marbella.
The visual language is coherent and appropriately premium, using editorial serif display typography with restrained uppercase navigation.
Reservation is present in the primary navigation and repeated through the hero CTA.
The location cue “PUERTO BANÚS · MARBELLA” is visible in the hero and supports geographic discovery.
The desktop and mobile layouts avoid horizontal overflow and retain a strong top-level reservation affordance.
The page structure and headline hierarchy are clear when the cookie dialog is dismissed.
The imagery, spacing and dark overlay create a warm, evening-oriented dining atmosphere consistent with the intended positioning.

aiReview.summary: This is not currently reviewable as a functioning premium real-estate website because both supplied captures show only a persistent loading screen. The objective metrics indicate that the delivery shell is fast and technically stable, but the user-facing business experience is absent: no brand proposition, listings, navigation, filters, imagery, trust content, or enquiry path is visible. The priority is to fix the rendering or hydration issue, then establish the complete property-discovery-to-enquiry journey before refining the visual system.
strengths: The deployment responds successfully with HTTP 200.
The objective scan reports strong loading performance, zero layout shift, no horizontal overflow, no console errors, and no failed network requests.
Viewport metadata, robots, sitemap, and image-alt checks are present, but these technical positives do not compensate for the absent rendered experience.
